q: Tell me about yourself and your relevant experience.
a:
Sure. I'm a delivery leader with 19 years of experience. And what makes me a bit different is that I bring two things together. I have deep technical roots, and I've owned the full business side of delivery.

Today, at NeuSix, I own five AI, digital twin and SaaS programs, for clients in four regions. I own them end to end: pre-sales, budget, client relationships, delivery and profit.

My career has really had three stages. First, seven years as a Technical Architect at DQ Entertainment. That's why I can still challenge an estimate or a design today. Second, delivery leadership at Deluxe, Hornbill and Cosmos-Maya. I delivered for Hollywood studios, and I turned around programs that were slipping. Third, AI and digital transformation. At Brane, I built the Philips X-ray digital twin from zero. At NeuSix, I lead programs with CEO-level sponsors.

Let me give you three results that show how I work. At Deluxe, I raised team productivity by 20%. At Hornbill, I cut delivery time by about 30%, and proved it with data. And on PaySFT, we lost half the team, but still delivered 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days. In total, I've delivered more than 30 platforms.

So in one line: I understand the technology, I own the business results, and I've delivered real AI. That's exactly what this role needs.

Likely follow-up: "Why are you looking for a change?"

I want to lead at a bigger scale: bigger accounts, bigger teams and a mature delivery setup. That's where my 19 years will make the biggest difference.

q: Can you talk about a challenging situation you faced at work and how you overcame it?
a:
My rule is simple. I never risk a client's live service to hit my own date. We move when we are ready, not when the calendar says so.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we had to take over Zolvit, a live AI legal platform, from the team that built it. Real customers used it every day. And the people who knew it best were leaving. For a legal platform, one wrong answer or one outage can damage the client's name.

So what did I do? First, I didn't switch over in one go. We did it in three steps. We watched their team work. Then we ran it while they watched us. Then we signed off formally. Second, I set clear readiness checks. We took full control only when the guides were written, we had all the access, monitoring was working, and we had practised the top incidents. Third, I protected the service after the switch. Support time was kept separate, so new work could never take it away. And fourth, I kept about 10% of the team's time for improvements, so the platform kept getting better.

And the result? We switched over with zero service disruption and no missed service levels. The client's customers didn't even notice the change.

So for me, with a live system, a safe handover beats a fast one every time. And in this role, I'd use the same playbook whenever we take over an account from another vendor.

Likely follow-up: "What would you do differently?"

I would write the readiness checks into the contract from day one. Then the handover date depends on being ready, and nobody can push it under pressure.

q: Explain a program you built from scratch. How did you establish the vision, success parameters and operating model?
a:
I build every program in the same order. First, one clear business goal. Then, how we will measure success. Then, how we will run the program. And the client's leaders sign off all three before we build anything.

Let me give you an example. At Brane, I built the Philips X-ray digital twin from zero. It predicts failures in X-ray machines in hospitals. When I started, there was no team, no plan and no definition of success. Philips wanted to stop fixing machines after they broke, and start fixing them before a hospital lost one.

So what did I do? First, I agreed a one-line goal: warn the service team early enough to plan a visit. Second, I agreed success at three levels. The business result was X days of early warning. The model had to be more than X% accurate. And the service engineers who would use it had to approve it. Third, I split the work into three stages: a proof of concept, a first version and a field trial. Each stage got money only after the one before it worked. And fourth, I set up one plan for all four teams, with weekly reviews, client demos every two weeks and a monthly steering meeting.

And the result? The program passed all three stages against the agreed targets. And problems came up in weekly reviews, not at the end.

So for me, when the goal and success are clear on day one, every decision after that becomes easier. That's how I'd launch every big program here.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client can't define success?"

I help them. I ask: which business number should change, by how much, and by when? If they still can't say, I suggest a short paid discovery first, not a build with no target.

q: If you joined tomorrow as Senior Delivery Manager, what would your first 100 days look like?
a:
My first 100 days follow three steps: listen, stabilise, then set the direction. But I don't wait 30 days to act. From week one, I fix what hurts the client most.

I base this on two real starts. At Cosmos-Maya, I had six months to fix several slipping programs. Leadership had no report they trusted, and nobody owned the risks. At PaySFT, the client was already escalating, so I had to act on day one.

So what did I do at Cosmos-Maya? In the first 30 days, I checked the health of every program, and fixed the most urgent issues at the same time. By day 60, I had one risk list with a name and a date on every item, one staffing plan for all programs, and one report leadership trusted. By day 90, we were tracking weekly results against milestones. And when things are urgent, I go faster. On PaySFT, the honest status went to the client in week one, and the new plan in week two.

And the result? At Cosmos-Maya, on-time milestones went from X% to Y%. On PaySFT, we delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days.

So for the first year here, I would commit to clear targets: on-time delivery above 85 to 90%, escalations cut in half, margin up 2 to 3 points, and two delivery leads ready for bigger accounts.

Likely follow-up: "What will you NOT do in the first 30 days?"

I won't change things that already work just to show I'm in charge. And I won't promise new dates to clients before I've checked the facts.

Likely follow-up: "Why should we pay at the top of the band?"

Because improving margin by 2 to 3 points, and growing even one account, is worth many times my package. And I have delivered results like that before.

q: How do you establish governance and a delivery operating model?
a:
Governance has one job: to help people make good decisions fast. I build it on four things: clear decision owners, a fixed meeting rhythm, one source of truth, and a way of working that fits each program.

Let me give you an example. When I took over the programs at NeuSix, I got five AI, digital twin and SaaS programs, and each one was run differently. Nobody knew who decided what. Risks lived in people's heads. And CEO-level sponsors were getting status updates instead of decisions.

So what did I do? First, I made it clear who decides what: the team, me, or the client's steering committee. Every risk got a name and a date. Second, I set a fixed rhythm: daily stand-ups, a weekly program review, and a monthly steering meeting. The pack went out two days before, and the actions within 24 hours. Third, all reports came from one risk list and one dashboard, so nobody argued about numbers. And fourth, I matched the method to the work: Scrum for new builds, Kanban for live platforms like Zolvit, and extra controls for AI agents.

And the result? It held up under pressure. When PaySFT lost half its team, we acted in week one and still delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days. At DP World, issues raised in steering turned into four new projects. And on-time milestones went from X% to Y%.

So for me, good governance doesn't slow delivery down. It speeds up decisions. Here, I'd run it inside your existing framework, with one rule: every meeting ends with a decision.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop governance becoming bureaucracy?"

Every meeting must end with a decision, or we cancel it. Reviews only cover red and amber items. And if a process doesn't change a result, I remove it.

Likely follow-up: "What about a project manager who hides red status?"

I make the status rules clear, so the colour isn't anyone's opinion. I praise people in public for raising red early. And if someone keeps hiding problems, I treat it as a performance issue.

q: A multi-region organisation has inconsistent processes, KPIs and governance. How do you build an operating model that scales but stays flexible?
a:
My rule is: fixed on what, flexible on how. Everything the client and leadership see is the same everywhere: the numbers, the status rules and the reports. How each team works day to day is their choice.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my programs served clients in the US, Europe, the Middle East and Asia Pacific, with about 60 to 70 people and four vendors. Green meant different things to different managers. Two clients even asked why their reports looked so different.

So what did I do? First, I set five standard numbers, with clear written rules. For example, red means the end date has slipped by more than 10%, or a blocker is older than five days. Second, I wrote one playbook together with the leads, based on what our best team already did. So they owned it. Third, I made Jira and Confluence the one source of truth, and added reporting rules into vendor contracts. And fourth, teams kept the freedom to choose Scrum or Kanban.

And the result? Within one quarter, we had one view of all programs. We saw risks two to three weeks earlier, time spent on status reports dropped by about half, and every client got the same quality of reporting.

So for me, standardise what the client sees, and free up how the team works. At 50 or more teams, I'd add quarterly planning across teams and protected time for technical debt.

Likely follow-up: "How do you handle a region that resists?"

I find out what they're trying to protect. If it really helps their client, I approve it as an exception. If it's just habit, I show them the numbers next to other regions.

Likely follow-up: "How would you know it's working?"

The gap between regions on the same numbers gets smaller every quarter, and client satisfaction goes up everywhere.

Likely follow-up: "What do you centralise and what do you leave local?"

I keep standards, tools and quality checks central. Client relationships, hiring and daily ways of working stay local.

q: A ₹500+ crore transformation across Cloud, Data, AI, Cyber, ERP and modernisation. How do you build the roadmap, manage dependencies and ensure business outcomes?
a:
I start from the business results and work backwards. I build the foundations first: cloud, security and data. I release money stage by stage, only when results come in. And each business leader owns their own benefits.

To be honest, I haven't run a 500 crore program. But I've led programs with many streams, like Philips and DP World, where cloud, data, IoT, AI and security ran on one plan. The same ideas work at a bigger size.

So what would I do? First, link every piece of work to one business goal. On Philips, everything linked to one goal: less machine downtime. If a feature didn't help that, it went down the list. Second, treat data as the biggest risk. In my programs, data causes more delays than the AI does. So data readiness is on the plan from day one. Third, run one plan for all streams. Otherwise every stream says green, while the points where they connect are red. And fourth, at this size, add a transformation office, a design authority, independent testing and a benefits tracker.

And the result? On Philips, the program passed all three stages on one plan. At DP World, the focus on business results led to four new projects, each with its own business case.

So for me, big programs fail on the data and where the teams connect. I plan for both from day one, and I move old systems in waves, not all at once.

Likely follow-up: "Which area would you start with?"

Security and the data platform, because everything else depends on them. AI comes last, once we can trust the data.

Likely follow-up: "How do you keep business units engaged over several years?"

I deliver something useful every quarter, and each business leader presents their own results at steering.

q: How frequently do you interact with clients, and what meetings do you attend?
a:
I talk to clients every day at the working level, and I meet their leaders on a fixed schedule. For me, the client relationship is the job, not an extra.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I'm the main delivery contact for client leaders on five programs, including CEO-level sponsors. At Brane, I was the delivery lead for Philips. My promise to every client is simple: you will never hear bad news from someone else first.

So what's my rhythm? First, every day: team stand-ups, and the client's product owner joins where agreed. Second, every week: a program review of progress, dependencies and risks. Third, every two weeks: a live demo of working software. On Philips, these mattered most, because leaders saw a working digital twin, not slides. Fourth, every month: a steering meeting on results, money and decisions. And I personally join every escalation and every decision on scope or budget.

And the result? Client leaders get decisions, not surprises. At DP World, these meetings became the place where new problems came up, and that led to four new projects.

So for me, the client should always hear bad news from me first. With senior clients here, I'd also add a monthly one-to-one with each sponsor, and a quarterly review of the value we delivered.

Likely follow-up: "How do you manage clients in different time zones?"

We meet in the hours when our time zones overlap, we share the early and late slots fairly, and we send written notes so nobody has to attend live.

q: How do you stay organised and manage your time across multiple programs?
a:
I run on a system, not on memory. And I spend my own time where the risk and the value are highest. Green programs run on the standard rhythm. Red programs get me.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run five programs at the same time. Each one has a different client, technology and deadline.

So how do I do it? First, every program has the same rhythm: daily stand-ups, a weekly review and a monthly steering meeting. Second, one risk list in Jira for all five programs. Third, clear delegation. Each lead runs their program day to day. I keep three things: client relationships, big risks, and decisions about money or scope. And fourth, I set priority by business impact. When PaySFT needed urgent help, I still protected Zolvit's live support team.

And the result? We recovered PaySFT and delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days. And Zolvit's live service was never affected. At Hornbill, the same discipline helped cut delivery time by about 30%.

So for me, when the system is right, I don't need to chase anyone. I can focus on the one or two accounts that really need me.

Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what to delegate?"

I keep client relationships, big risks and decisions on money or scope. Everything else goes to the leads, with clear ownership and a weekly check-in.

Likely follow-up: "How do you make sure multiple projects are delivered on time, within budget and to quality standards?"

I use the same system on every project, with early warnings for time, money and quality. Every program has a starting plan and budget, a weekly review of schedule, spend and bugs, and one risk list. Quality is built in with automated tests, not checked at the end. And when one project slips, I act early, like on PaySFT.

q: How do you balance mature BAU operations with innovation?
a:
The live service always comes first. But improvement work gets its own protected time. If it has to fight support tickets every week, it never happens, and the client slowly loses value.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we took over Zolvit, an AI legal platform. Once it went live, support tickets could easily have used up all our time.

So what did I do? First, service levels came first. We moved to Kanban, and support work always took priority. On a legal platform, correct answers matter more than new features. Second, I split the team's time clearly: support, change requests, urgent fixes, and about 10% just for improvements. Third, we found improvement ideas in the support work itself: repeat tickets, manual work, and feedback from customers and lawyers. And fourth, for AI ideas, we started with one small trial, like AI sorting of tickets, and only scaled what worked.

And the result? The service stayed stable, we met service levels every month, and repeat tickets went down by X%. The client kept getting improvements, not just fixes.

So for me, improvement needs its own budget, even a small one, or urgent work always wins. I also show these improvements to the client every quarter, because that's how a support contract grows into new work.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client won't pay for improvement time?"

I show them what not improving already costs: the repeat tickets and manual work they pay for today. Usually, the improvement pays for itself within a few months.

q: Tell me about a program that was in crisis or at risk. How did you stabilize it?
a:
In a crisis, I don't rush to fix things in week one. I find the real cause, make it visible, and give it an owner. When many programs are red at once, there are usually only one or two shared causes.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, leadership gave me six months to stabilise several running programs. Deadlines were being missed. Nobody trusted the status reports. Nobody owned the risks. And people were moved between projects every day.

So what did I do? First, I diagnosed before fixing. I reviewed every program's goals, people, money and delivery, to find what was really causing the delays. Second, I fixed the system, not the symptoms: one risk list with a name and a date on every item, one staffing plan for all programs, and a clear escalation path. Third, I changed the mindset. The teams saw the risk list as paperwork. So I showed them how one risk, left open for weeks, had become the exact delay we were facing. After that, they owned it.

And the result? By day 30, we knew where every program stood. By day 60, leadership had one view they trusted. By day 90, we tracked weekly results. On-time milestones went from X% to Y%, and escalations dropped from X to Y.

So for me, when many programs are in trouble, find the shared problem first. Here, I'd rank red programs by revenue and contract risk, and put my strongest leads on the top ones.

Likely follow-up: "What was the hardest part?"

The mindset. A process is easy to set up. People only used it once they saw it prevent a real problem.

Likely follow-up: "What if you take over a project that is already three months late? How do you recover it without hurting quality or morale?"

First, I take two weeks to understand the real work left. Then I agree a new plan with the client, built on the must-haves. I keep testing in the plan, because testing is never the buffer. I clear blockers every day, and I don't make overtime the plan. Early wins rebuild trust on both sides. That's how we recovered PaySFT and delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days.

q: How do you manage delivery delays and missed commitments?
a:
Bad news early is a gift. Bad news late is a crisis. When we miss a commitment, I own it openly, I re-plan around what matters most, and I give the client a clear decision, not just a new date.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I was running PaySFT, a real estate platform. Suddenly, we lost about half the team. Dates started slipping, the client escalated, and their trust was falling fast.

So what did I do? First, I owned it in writing in week one: what went wrong, why, and what we would change. I didn't hide behind the team loss. Second, I re-planned around the must-haves for launch, using the team we actually had. Third, I gave the client a clear choice, including a costed option of ₹32 lakh to deliver everything. So they decided with the facts. And fourth, I tightened delivery: daily stand-ups with notes, a name and a date on every risk, and steering meetings focused on decisions. Any new delay showed up within days.

And the result? We delivered 125 APIs plus the Broker and Buyer mobile apps in 45 days. The escalation closed, and the client trusted us again.

So for me, a missed commitment is a trust problem first, and a schedule problem second. Senior clients should always hear about a delay from me first, with options and my recommendation.

Likely follow-up: "When do you add more people to a late project?"

Last. First I cut the work down to the must-haves and remove blockers. New people slow a team down for the first few weeks.

Likely follow-up: "How do you know the recovery is real?"

When we hit the new plan two or three weeks in a row, and the number of bugs stays flat or goes down.

Likely follow-up: "What if the project is behind schedule but the client still expects delivery on the planned date?"

I tell the client early, with facts and options, never on the day. On PaySFT, I wrote an honest note in week one, cut the plan to the must-haves, and gave a costed ₹32 lakh option. We delivered in 45 days. Clients can accept a new plan. They can't accept a surprise.

q: How do you identify the root cause of a delivery problem?
a:
I diagnose before I fix. The data shows me where the problem is. The people closest to the work tell me why. And I keep going until I find a problem in the system, not a person to blame.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, programs were slipping. Leadership could see the symptoms, but nobody could explain the cause. I had to find it before the business spent more money on the wrong fix. So I spent the first 30 days diagnosing, not fixing.

So what did I do? First, I looked at the data: goals, money and delivery for every program, side by side. A program can look on time while it burns through the budget. Second, I talked to the people, and kept asking why. Why are we missing milestones? Because teams are blocked. Why? Because key people are shared. Why? Because there is no shared staffing plan. Third, I tested the cause. A real root cause must explain all the symptoms. Ours did: no single risk list, no shared staffing plan, and no escalation path.

And the result? We fixed the system, not the people. By day 60, leadership had one status view they trusted. By day 90, we tracked weekly results.

So for me, when delivery fails, it's usually the system, not the people. I always confirm the real cause before I approve money for a fix.

Likely follow-up: "What if the cause is one underperforming person?"

First I check if the system set them up to fail. If not, I talk to them directly and privately, with clear expectations, support and a deadline.

q: How do you manage dependencies across teams and programs?
a:
A dependency without an owner and a date is just a hope. I put every dependency on one plan, give it an owner on both sides, and make the handover a goal both teams share.

Let me give you an example. On the Philips digital twin, the AI team couldn't move without machine data. And that data came from hardware partly outside our control. Four teams depended on each other, and hardware never moves at software speed.

So what did I do? First, I put all four teams on one plan, so every handover was visible. Second, we kept one shared risk list with the client, with an owner and a need-by date for every dependency. Third, the data and AI teams signed off integration together. Done meant working together, not just each part on its own. And fourth, we signed a data agreement with the Philips engineers on fields, formats and timing. So nobody built on guesses.

And the result? The program passed all three stages on one plan. And integration problems showed up in weekly reviews, not at the end.

So for me, plan integration as a shared goal, not as a handover at the end. In cloud and microservices programs, the rule is the same: agree the interfaces early, give each one an owner, and test them together every sprint.

Likely follow-up: "What about a dependency on the client or a third party?"

It goes on the risk list with a need-by date, and it's visible at steering. If it slips, I escalate through the client sponsor, with a dated request and the cost of the delay.

Likely follow-up: "What if none of those teams, vendors or business units report to you?"

Then I lead with a shared goal and clear agreements, not authority. I ask the sponsor to confirm the goal and my role. I agree simple rules with each lead, like need-by dates and escalation within 48 hours. Everyone sees the same plan every week. For vendors, it's in the contract. That's how our teams and Philips' engineers worked to one plan.

q: How do you manage conflicting timelines and shared resources across programs?
a:
I protect what can't move. I solve shortages inside the program first. And when there's a real trade-off, the business decides with clear facts. I never quietly take people from one program to save another.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my five programs share the same AI, cloud and engineering people. When PaySFT lost about half its team, it needed help urgently. But Zolvit, a live platform with service levels, still needed its full support team.

So what did I do? First, I protected the live service. Nobody touched Zolvit's support team, because a live service always comes before a new build. Second, I solved PaySFT inside PaySFT. I re-planned it around the must-haves, for the team it had. Third, I made the trade-off the client's decision, with a costed ₹32 lakh option to deliver everything. And fourth, I kept any knock-on risks visible in the weekly review.

And the result? PaySFT delivered 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days. And Zolvit's service levels were never affected.

So for me, priority comes from business value and commitments, not from who shouts loudest. Here, I'd keep one capacity view across accounts, with rare skills flagged, and one open scoring rule everyone agrees.

Likely follow-up: "Two senior stakeholders have conflicting priorities, and both say theirs is business-critical. How do you reach a decision?"

I meet each one separately first, to understand the business result behind their request. Often the conflict is in the solution, not the goal. Then I put both options on one page: value, cost of delay and risk. Often there's an order that works for both. If not, I take it to the leader they both report to, with my recommendation. And we write the decision down.

Likely follow-up: "What if a business leader rejects the scoring?"

Leadership agrees the scoring rule before any decision. Then we only discuss the facts that go into it, not the result.

Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what to defer?"

With the same open scoring rule, agreed with the sponsors. So it's a business decision, not mine alone.

Likely follow-up: "How do you manage resource allocation when multiple projects need the same critical team members?"

I keep one view of capacity, protect live services first, and use an agreed rule for the rest. On PaySFT, I didn't move Zolvit's engineers. I re-planned PaySFT and gave the client a costed option. Over time, I train people across skills, so we never depend on one person.

q: A critical transformation is near go-live with open risks and gaps. Business leaders want the original date. How do you decide on readiness?
a:
Go-live should never be a fight between opinions. I use a clear go or no-go checklist, signed by each lead. Then I give leaders options, not just yes or no. The business owns the risk. My job is to make the risk impossible to misunderstand.

Let me give you an example. At Jazeera Airport, we built a digital twin of the terminal. The launch was tied to a leadership event, so the date could not move. Two weeks before launch, live cameras for 2 of the 6 zones were blocked by security approvals outside our control.

So what did I do? First, we checked readiness against 22 go or no-go points, signed by each lead. Nearly ready became: these four checks are red, and here's why. Second, I took four options to the sponsor, and recommended a phased launch: four zones live on the date, and clearly labelled recorded video for the other two. Third, the sponsor accepted the risk in writing, and we ran two full rehearsals with a backup. And fourth, I pushed the blocked approval through the client's IT head, with a clear date.

And the result? The launch went ahead on the date with no issues. All zones went live three weeks later, with zero production incidents.

So for me, don't fight the date. Change what goes live on the date, and get the risk decision in writing.

Likely follow-up: "What if leadership insists on full scope?"

Then it's their decision. We write it down, with the risk clearly stated, a rollback plan and named owners after launch. I escalate once, clearly, but I don't block a fair business decision.

Likely follow-up: "What if a red item is a safety or compliance risk?"

Then it's a hard stop. That part does not go live until it's fixed, and I escalate straight away.

q: A client demands faster delivery with the same budget, quality and scope. How do you reach a sustainable outcome?
a:
I don't say yes, and I don't say no. I ask why the date matters. There's usually a business event behind it, and that event rarely needs everything.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, the client for Vigilant, an AI sales platform, asked us to launch six weeks early for an industry event. And they wanted the same budget.

So what did I do? First, I asked what they needed to show on stage. The answer was just two AI features: researching sales leads and drafting outreach. Second, we delivered those two features early, fully tested and ready for real use. Everything else came in phase two, on the original date. Third, we shared the effort. We reused parts from an earlier build, which saved about three weeks. And the client agreed to give feedback within 48 hours. And fourth, we put it all in a change note, signed by their head of product.

And the result? They demoed it live at the event and got new sales leads. Phase two went live on the original date, with the same budget and the same margin for us.

So for me, faster for the same money usually means: I need one specific thing by one specific date. Find that thing.

Likely follow-up: "What if they really need everything earlier?"

Then it needs more people or more money, and I show exactly how much. I won't promise it at the same price and then cut testing.

q: A strategic client is unhappy because of missed milestones and poor communication. How do you rebuild confidence?
a:
Trust comes back when you keep promises, not when you make them. I find out what each client leader really cares about, I report results instead of activity, and I make small promises and keep every one.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we were building a warehouse digital twin. We had missed two milestones, and the operations head had stopped coming to our reviews. When I looked closer, I saw the real problem. Our sponsor was the innovation team, but the real users were warehouse operations, and we had never properly involved them.

So what did I do? First, I went to the real user. I met the operations head and asked: what would make this useful to you on Monday morning? Equipment use and waiting times became our top priority. Second, I replaced status reports with a one-page business update and a live demo every two weeks, on their own warehouse data. Third, we kept a joint scorecard of milestones, issues and decisions owed by each side. And fourth, every two weeks we made small promises with dates, and kept every one.

And the result? Within two months, the operations head was coming to demos and asking for features. The sponsor used our demo in their own leadership review. And later, we won four new projects.

So for me, the person who pays is not always the person who decides. Find the real user, and trust follows.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client is also at fault?"

I own our part first, because that's the only way they'll listen. Then we keep a shared decision list with deadlines, so late decisions become visible without blame.

Likely follow-up: "What if the problem is one person on your team?"

I change the person on the account quickly and respectfully. The relationship matters more than any one role.

Likely follow-up: "What approach do you follow to manage client expectations and maintain long-term relationships?"

Clear expectations at the start, no surprises along the way, and value beyond the contract. At DP World, this turned steering meetings into the place where new problems came up, and the account grew into four new projects.

q: How do you measure customer satisfaction and delivery success?
a:
I measure delivery success against goals we agreed before we started. And I read client happiness in three ways: what clients say, what they do, and how their leaders engage.

I've seen projects meet every deadline while the client stayed unhappy, and the other way round. So one number is never enough. I need an honest picture of both, early enough to act.

Here's what I do. First, I agree success up front. On Philips, we agreed three levels before any build: the business result, the stages and model accuracy. So success was never a matter of opinion. Second, I ask every month. At NeuSix, client concerns are a fixed item at every steering meeting, so issues come up monthly, not at renewal. Third, I watch behaviour. When DP World started sharing their business problems with us, that told me more than any survey. On PaySFT, I knew trust was back when we stopped talking about escalations and started talking about the roadmap.

And the result? At DP World, trust turned into four new projects. On PaySFT, the client trusted us again after the 45-day delivery.

So for me, success is meeting the agreed goals. Real satisfaction is being trusted with more work. Here, I'd track satisfaction every quarter, next to renewals, escalations and account growth.

Likely follow-up: "What if KPIs are green but the client is unhappy?"

Then we're measuring the wrong things. It's a watermelon report: green outside, red inside. I ask the sponsor directly what success looks like now, and I change what we report.

q: How do you manage long-term clients where informal commitments have developed?
a:
I protect the goodwill, but I make informal requests visible. Free favours that nobody records slowly eat our margin and tire out the team.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the relationship was strong. Over time, the operations team got used to sending quick requests on WhatsApp or by phone. One Thursday evening, they asked for a new dock layout and an updated simulation by Monday.

So what did I do? First, I checked the impact on scope, the team's time and the plan. Second, I gave them clear options: do it by Monday and move other work, deliver a smaller version first, or add people through a paid change request. They chose one and confirmed it in writing. Third, I made it a system: a weekly slot for quick changes with fixed capacity, and one priority list for every request. And fourth, I started checking unbilled work every month, because that's the first sign of margin leaking.

And the result? The client still got quick changes, just planned ones. The hidden weekend work stopped. And the relationship grew into four new projects.

So for me, keep the goodwill, but make the promises visible.

Likely follow-up: "Won't the client feel you're less flexible?"

No. They still get quick changes, just planned ones. And everything else becomes more reliable.

Likely follow-up: "How do you manage scope changes when a client asks for additional features during an ongoing project?"

I never just say no, and I never quietly do it for free. I check the impact and give options: swap it for something of the same size, deliver a smaller version first, or add it through a paid change. At DP World, this made the relationship stronger, not weaker.

q: What business KPIs do you track?
a:
I look at two sides. The client's business: is our work moving their numbers? And our business: margin and account growth. A program that's on time but moves neither is not a success.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the same operational problems kept coming up in our steering meetings: no live view of warehouse space, damaged goods found too late, slow robot routes and busy conveyors. I saw a chance to link our delivery to their business results, and grow the account.

So what did I do? First, with my architects, I turned those problems into four computer vision use cases: space monitoring, damage detection, robot route planning and conveyor flow. Second, I backed each one with an ROI workbook. So we talked about money saved, not technology. Third, I measured success with the client's own numbers: space used, damage rates, robot efficiency and conveyor throughput.

And the result? Four new use cases, each with a clear business case, a proposal worth X, and a package we could reuse for other logistics clients.

So for me, the best business number is delivery that creates the next piece of work. For each account here, I'd track margin, revenue growth, new work won through delivery, and the client's own results.

Likely follow-up: "What margin do you aim for?"

It depends on the account and the contract type. I protect it with honest estimates, strict change control and the right team mix.

q: You are meeting milestones, but profit has dropped because of rework, low utilisation, extra scope and vendor costs. How do you fix it without hurting quality?
a:
Margin problems are usually quality problems in disguise. I find exactly where the money is going, fix rework and unbilled work first, and only then look at the team.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, I ran technology delivery for big Hollywood films like Black Panther, Doctor Strange and Thor: Ragnarok. We met every studio deadline, but costs were running 18% over plan.

So what did I do? First, I made rework visible. I tracked how much work the studio approved the first time. About 35% of our effort was going into redoing work. Second, I built quality in: our own review before anything went to the studio, and a short checklist to clear doubts before work started. Third, I invested in people and automation. I coached the team and automated the repeated steps. And fourth, I stopped the leaks. I put three vendor schedules into one plan, and made sure every studio change was recorded and billed.

And the result? Productivity went up 20%. First-time approval went from about 60% to about 80%. Costs came back to within 5% of plan. And the studios were happier.

So for me, cutting quality to save money is the most expensive decision you can make.

Likely follow-up: "What healthy numbers do you aim for?"

About 80 to 85% billable time, less than 5% unbilled work, less than 10% rework, and senior people focused on design and review.

Likely follow-up: "Which lever do you pull first?"

The one with the biggest value and the least client impact. Usually that's unbilled work, because that's money for work we've already done.

Likely follow-up: "How often would you review the bridge?"

Every month for each account, and every quarter for leadership.

Likely follow-up: "What if the project is technically successful but costs are over the approved budget?"

I tell the sponsor early, with a forecast and a clear breakdown of where the extra cost comes from. Then I use the levers that don't hurt results: push back low-value scope, bill the free changes, fix the team mix and cut waste. If there's still a gap, the sponsor chooses: more budget, less scope, or more time. That's how I handled PaySFT, with the ₹32 lakh option.

q: What delivery KPIs do you track?
a:
I keep it to six or eight numbers on one page. And I always mix early warning signs with results. Because if you only track results, you find out you've failed after it's too late to fix it.

Let me give you an example. In a few of my programs, leaders only found out about problems on the delivery day. Or people said things had improved, but nobody could actually prove it.

So what did I do? First, at Hornbill, I measured how long work really took before I changed anything. That gave us a starting point. Second, at Deluxe, I tracked speed and rework together, so nobody could look fast by shipping poor work. Third, at Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that turned amber the moment a team started falling behind. And on accounts with real engineering, I add the four DORA numbers: how often we release, how long a change takes to go live, how often a release fails, and how fast we recover.

And the result? At Hornbill, delivery got about 30% faster, and we could prove it. At Deluxe, productivity went up 20%. And at Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, numbers are there to help us decide, not to fill reports.

Likely follow-up: "If you could track only one number?"

What we promised versus what we actually delivered. That's exactly what the client feels.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop teams gaming the metrics?"

I always pair a speed number with a quality number. And I use the numbers to ask questions, never to punish people. Once people stop being scared of the numbers, they stop gaming them.

Likely follow-up: "Which metrics would you use to predict future outcomes, not just report the past, and how do you turn them into executive decisions?"

I look at the trend, not just today's number. Is what we deliver dropping against what we promise? Is scope growing faster than we finish work? Are risks staying open too long? Are bugs going up? From that, I give leaders a range of dates, not one fixed date. And every red sign comes with a decision I need from them. At Discreet Arts, that's how we saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

q: How do you manage risks and escalations?
a:
Every big risk gets three things: an owner, a plan, and a trigger. The trigger tells us exactly when to switch to plan B. And when I escalate, I always bring options and my recommendation, not just a problem.

Let me give you three quick examples from NeuSix, because risks come in different shapes. There's technical risk, there's operational risk, and there's commercial risk.

First, a handover risk on Zolvit. We only took over the live platform once the agreed readiness checks were met. Not before. Second, an AI risk on Vigilant. From day one, the agents had limits on what they could do, a person approved anything sensitive, and they had to pass a minimum score to go live. And third, a commercial risk on PaySFT. When we lost half the team, I wrote an honest note to the client in week one, with a costed ₹32 lakh option. And my escalation rule is simple. 48 hours to the program manager, five days to me, and then the steering committee.

And the result? Zolvit moved over with zero disruption. Vigilant's agents went live safely. And PaySFT delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days.

So for me, a risk list tells you what might happen. A trigger tells you when to act.

Likely follow-up: "Tell me about a risk you missed."

Honestly, on Philips, early on, I let the team build on guesses about the machine data. When the real data came, it didn't match, and we lost time. Since then, a signed data agreement is a day-one task on every program I run (see question 33).

Likely follow-up: "Give me an example of a trigger."

Sure. If the vendor's integration isn't in testing by the 15th, we switch to the backup and I call their account director. It's specific, it has a date, and somebody owns it.

Likely follow-up: "How do you identify and manage delivery risks before they affect project outcomes?"

I watch for early signs, not late results. A dependency with no date. A risk that's been open too long. Bugs going up. Delivery dropping against what we promised. On Philips, that's why the data agreement became a day-one task. And at Discreet Arts, the amber warning showed us delays two to three weeks early.

q: How do you identify and manage vendor and budget risks?
a:
Vendor problems and budget problems usually turn up together. So I deal with both the same way: clear owners, the contract as the referee, estimates from real data, and money problems raised early. Never late.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, several vendors worked on the same studio films, and handovers between them kept causing arguments. And at NeuSix, I own the profit and loss on programs with four vendors, across AWS, GCP and Azure.

So what did I do? First, every vendor deliverable got an owner, a date and an agreed scope. When there was an argument, we settled it with the contract, not with opinions. Second, I put every vendor on the same rules as our own team: the same sprint calendar, the same quality checks, the same definition of done. Third, on budget, I tracked spend against plan every week, and I never quietly absorbed extra cost. On PaySFT, I gave the client a costed ₹32 lakh option instead.

And the result? At Deluxe, putting three vendor schedules into one plan helped bring costs back within 5% of plan. On PaySFT, the costed option protected our margin and the client's trust at the same time.

So for me, surprises are what kill budgets. So I make money problems visible early.

Likely follow-up: "A strategic vendor misses critical milestones and puts a major product launch at risk. How do you handle the contract, the recovery and the communication?"

Three things at once. On the contract side, I check the milestones and penalties, and I send a formal written notice, so our position is protected. On recovery, I meet their leadership the same week, agree a recovery plan with dates, and track it daily. And I quietly start the backup, like another vendor or doing it ourselves. On communication, the sponsor hears it from me first, with options. I use penalties last, because the goal is to save the launch, not to win the argument.

q: What is your experience with AI agents or agentic AI?
a:
Yes, I've taken AI agents into real production. And for me, the big lesson is this. Agentic AI is not a tool you switch on. It's a new kind of worker, and it needs rules, supervision and a budget, just like a person does.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, we built AI agents for Vigilant, an AI sales platform. The agents research sales leads, and they draft outreach emails and proposals for real customers. So a mistake here goes straight to a real customer, under the client's name.

So what did I do? First, limits. Each agent had a fixed list of tools it was allowed to use, and nothing else. Second, a person in the loop. No email or proposal went out until a person approved it. Third, testing. Every agent was scored on real cases, and it only went live after it passed the agreed score. And fourth, visibility. We logged every action the agent took, why it took it, and what each task cost.

And the result? The agents went live with all the controls from day one. The client demoed them live at an industry event, and got new sales leads from it. And I've also delivered AI on Zolvit's legal platform, the Philips digital twin and DP World's computer vision.

So for me, you don't just switch an AI agent on. You control it. And honestly, those controls are exactly what make a senior client comfortable saying yes.

Likely follow-up: "Explain an AI agent simply."

A normal AI answers a question. An agent actually does things, like searching, updating a record or sending an email, to finish a task. That's why it needs limits and a person checking it.

q: Have you used tools like GitHub Copilot or Codex in delivery?
a:
Yes, and getting people to use the tools was only half the job. The other half was using AI safely with the client's code and data. So I set the rules before we started, not after something went wrong.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, our teams build AI products, so of course they wanted AI coding assistants on client work too. But we were working with client code and client data, so the risk was real.

So what did I do? I set four simple rules. One, only approved tools, on business licences, and with the client's okay where needed. Two, no confidential data in public or free tools. Ever. Three, a person reviews everything the AI writes before it's used. And four, AI-written code goes through exactly the same tests, code reviews and security scans as everything else.

And the result? The client was comfortable with us using AI in delivery, and we had zero data incidents. We got the speed, without taking on the risk.

So for me, speed from AI only counts if the client can trust it. And I'd agree those rules in writing with every client before we start.

Likely follow-up: "What gain did you see?"

[Give your real number], measured before and after, the way I explain in question 28. Without a starting point, any number is just a guess.

q: How would you measure productivity before and after adopting AI?
a:
I always measure speed and quality together, against a starting point. Because if we get faster but the bugs go up, that's not productivity. That's just moving the problem down the line.

Let me give you an example. I've done this twice. At Hornbill, I proved a 30% improvement against a starting point. And at NeuSix, when we brought in AI coding tools. And the trap is this. It's easy to claim AI made us faster. Lines of code, or how much people use the tool, prove nothing.

So what did I do? First, I measured before changing anything. How long work takes, how many bugs reach the client, how much rework we do, and how long code reviews take. Second, I compared fairly. Similar work, similar team, same period. Ideally, one team uses the tool and one doesn't. And third, I always showed the numbers side by side: speed next to bugs and rework, plus a quick survey of how the developers felt.

And the result? At Hornbill, that's why I can honestly say delivery got about 30% faster. And at NeuSix, AI-written code went through the same quality checks, so any speed we gained came with the same quality.

So for me, if you don't measure before, you can't prove anything after.

Likely follow-up: "What if quality drops?"

We pause, and fix the process first. Usually that means tighter review rules for AI-written code, before we roll it out any further.

q: How would you encourage AI adoption if the team is resistant?
a:
You can't order people to use AI. You have to win them over. So I find out what each person is actually worried about, I turn the biggest doubters into owners, and I use the tools myself, in front of everyone.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, when we brought in AI coding assistants, two of my senior engineers didn't trust AI-written code at all. And some of the others were quietly worried about their jobs. Now, if my best engineers say no, the rest of the team follows them.

So what did I do? First, I listened. Was the worry about quality? Job security? Time? A bad experience before? Each one needs a different answer. Second, I made the two doubters the owners. I asked them to write the review rules for AI-written code. Suddenly it was their standard, not mine. Third, I was honest with the team. I told them, the risk isn't AI. The risk is not learning it. And fourth, I planned learning time into the sprints, and we trained on their real work, not on demos.

And the result? The doubters became the people setting the bar, and the rest of the team followed. Use went up, and quality stayed the same.

So for me, people use AI when they see it's useful to them. You can't force it.

Likely follow-up: "What if someone still refuses?"

I don't force the tool. But I expect the same results as the rest of the team. And honestly, once they see their colleagues saving time, they usually try it.

q: How would you move a program from a traditional SDLC toward an agentic development lifecycle?
a:
Three big things change. Requirements become examples. Testing becomes scoring. And running the system becomes constant monitoring. So delivery turns into one continuous loop: build, test, monitor, improve.

Let me give you an example. I've been through this on our AI products at NeuSix, Zolvit and Vigilant. And what we found is that normal pass or fail testing just doesn't work for AI, because AI doesn't give the same answer every time.

So what did I do? First, requirements as examples. On Zolvit, we built a set of real legal questions with correct answers agreed by legal experts. That set became the requirement. Second, testing as scoring. On Vigilant, every agent had to hit an agreed minimum score on real cases before release, and that check runs automatically in the pipeline. And third, running it as monitoring. We logged what the agents did and what each task cost, and the next sprint was planned from that data.

And the result? Agents only went live after passing the agreed score, with accuracy above X%, and cost and behaviour were tracked from day one.

So for me, it's build, test, monitor, improve, all in one loop. And it fits right into DevOps. Your automated tests simply grow into automated AI scoring.

Likely follow-up: "What stays the same?"

Code reviews, security checks and release control. AI changes how we build and test, but we still need the same engineering discipline.

q: What do you consider when managing risk in AI delivery, especially in healthcare and finance?
a:
In healthcare and finance, an AI mistake can hurt a patient, a legal case, or somebody's money. So I manage four risks very clearly: the data, the model, the decision, and compliance. And I plan for the day the model is wrong.

Let me give you an example. I've worked in two sensitive areas. Healthcare, with Philips, where the data came from X-ray machines in hospitals. And legal, with Zolvit, where the platform gave legal answers to real customers.

So what did I do? First, data. On Philips, data quality, removing personal details and secure transfer were tracked as program risks from day one. Second, the model. Model accuracy was a formal pass mark at every stage. Third, the decision. On Zolvit, correct answers came before new features, and a person checked the sensitive answers. And fourth, compliance. Compliance people and subject experts were in from the start, not at the end.

And the result? Philips passed all three stages against the agreed accuracy targets. And in finance, it's the same ideas, plus that sector's rules, like RBI guidelines and model risk management. I also build privacy in from day one: GDPR, India's DPDP Act, HIPAA where it applies, and an eye on the EU AI Act.

So for me, in sensitive areas, the question isn't if the model will be wrong. It's what happens when it is.

Likely follow-up: "How do you explain an AI decision to a regulator?"

We keep a record of what data the model used and why it decided what it did. We keep every model version with its test results. And a person signs off the sensitive decisions.

q: Leadership wants to transform delivery with Jira, Azure DevOps, ServiceNow, Power BI, automation and AI forecasting. How do you design it?
a:
Honestly, tools come last. First, I decide which decisions the data has to help with. Then I get everyone working the same way, so the data is clean. Only then do I build dashboards and forecasting. And I prove it on one account before rolling it out.

Let me give you an example. I've done this twice. At Discreet Arts, leaders only heard about delays on the delivery day. And at NeuSix, our teams and vendors were all reporting in different tools, so nobody had one picture.

So what did I do? First, at Discreet Arts, I built a progress dashboard that warned us early when a team fell behind. Second, at NeuSix, I made Jira and Confluence the one place for everything, and every team, vendors included, used the same workflow steps and fields. And third, I'm honest about tools. I haven't used ServiceNow hands-on, but the rule doesn't change. Standard work first, dashboards second.

And the result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier. At NeuSix, we got one view of all programs, and time spent on reports dropped by about half.

So for me, a dashboard is only as good as the data behind it. My target design would be Jira or Azure DevOps for the work, ServiceNow for incidents and changes, Power BI as one view for leaders, and AI forecasting that gives a range of dates from real delivery data.

Likely follow-up: "How would you know it worked?"

Forecasts getting more accurate, managers spending about half the time on reports, risks found earlier, and leaders no longer asking for separate status slides.

Likely follow-up: "What's the biggest risk in a program like this?"

Messy data. If we don't standardise how people work first, the dashboards will look great, and be wrong.

q: Tell me about a failure. What went wrong, and what did you learn?
a:
On the Philips digital twin, I let the team start building on guesses about the machine data. When the real data arrived, it didn't match, and we lost time. That was my call, and I own it. But the lesson from it is something I still do on every single program.

Let me tell you what happened. Early on, we were under pressure to show progress, and the machine data wasn't ready yet. So I approved building on assumptions, so the team wouldn't sit idle. Then the real data came in, the fields and timings were different, and integration slipped by X weeks.

So what did I do? First, I told the client straight away, at the next steering meeting, with the impact and a recovery plan. Before it became a missed milestone. Second, I fixed the real cause. We signed a data agreement with the Philips engineers on fields, formats and timing, and we tracked data readiness with an owner on both sides. And third, I recovered the plan. We changed the order of the work and won back X of the Y weeks.

And the result? The program went on to pass all three stages. And every program I've run since starts with a data agreement on day one. I teach it to every lead I coach.

So for me, the best failure stories end with a rule you still follow today. And I think a senior leader has to be comfortable saying, this part was my mistake.

Likely follow-up: "Would you make the same decision again?"

No. Starting early was right. Starting without a data agreement was wrong. Today, I'd let the team build against a signed format and sample data.

q: How do you mentor and develop delivery leads, program managers and architects?
a:
My job is to build leaders, not followers. So I give people real responsibility with a safety net, and I teach them the part of the job they can't see yet. Architects learn to think about money and risk. Project managers learn to think about clients and margin.

Let me give you an example. I spent seven years coaching technical teams as an architect at DQ Entertainment. Later, at Hornbill, I built a team of delivery leads. When I joined, they were always firefighting, and every single decision came to me. That doesn't scale.

So what did I do? First, monthly one-to-ones about their growth, not about status. Second, stretch with a safety net. A lead runs the client meeting while I'm in the room, and I give feedback afterwards. Third, real ownership. Each lead owned a program end to end, with clear decision rights. And fourth, I taught the hidden parts. I moved from architect to delivery leader myself, so I can show an architect how to talk about cost, and a project manager how to read a profit and loss report.

And the result? At Hornbill, the leads ran several programs without me in the room, and delivery got about 30% faster.

So for me, my goal is to be a little less needed every quarter. Here, I'd aim to have two leads ready for bigger accounts in my first year, and a successor for every key role.

Likely follow-up: "A strong performer who is hard to work with?"

I give them clear, private feedback on the behaviour and its impact, and I make it part of their growth goals. At a senior level, results aren't enough. How you get them matters too.

q: How do you manage offshore, onshore and hybrid teams across time zones?
a:
Distance isn't the real problem. Unclear ownership is. So I set clear roles in each location, a written handover every day, fair meeting times, and one standard for everybody, vendors included.

Let me give you an example. I've worked this way most of my career. At Deluxe, we delivered for Hollywood studios from India. At Anibrain, we worked to fixed global release dates. And at NeuSix today, I work with clients in four regions. The client should feel one team, wherever people sit.

So what did I do? First, clear roles. Client-facing leads sit close to the client, and most building and testing happens offshore. Second, follow the sun. We write a short handover at the end of each day, so work keeps moving while the other side sleeps. Third, fair meetings. We meet in the overlap hours, we take turns with the bad slots, and we always send written notes. And fourth, one standard: same sprint calendar, same definition of done, same tools.

And the result? At Deluxe, we met every studio deadline while productivity went up 20%. And at NeuSix, every client gets the same quality of reporting, in every region.

So for me, it's one team, many locations, one standard. And I adjust to each culture. The US wants fast updates. Germany wants detailed plans. The UK values clear writing.

Likely follow-up: "How do you keep remote people engaged?"

Regular one-to-ones, praise in front of the client, and real chances for offshore people to work with the client directly.

q: How do you build compliance (ISO 27001, ISO 27701, SOC 2, GDPR) into delivery?
a:
Compliance is cheapest when you build it in on day one, and most expensive when you bolt it on at the end. So security and privacy are part of my definition of done, my release pipeline and my go-live checklist.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, the data came from medical machines in hospitals. And on Zolvit, the platform handled legal data. So protecting sensitive data was not optional, and we still had to deliver fast.

So what did I do? First, data. On Philips, removing personal details and getting data access approved were planned steps in the main plan, not afterthoughts. Second, access. People got only the access they needed, and we reviewed it regularly. Third, the pipeline. Security scans ran automatically on every build. And fourth, evidence. We collected audit evidence as we went, not in a panic just before the audit.

And the result? We delivered on sensitive hospital and legal data without a security incident, and audits weren't a fire drill.

So for me, build it in, don't bolt it on. And in simple words: ISO 27001 is the security system, 27701 adds privacy, SOC 2 Type 2 proves the controls work over time, and under GDPR a serious breach goes to the regulator within 72 hours.

Likely follow-up: "First hour of a data breach?"

Stop it spreading. Tell our security team and the client straight away. Keep the evidence. And write down the facts as we go. Under GDPR, the regulator may need to know within 72 hours.

q: How do you balance DevOps speed with ITIL control?
a:
Honestly, they're not opposites. Good automation gives you speed and control at the same time. Low-risk changes go through automatic checks. High-risk changes get a proper review. And live systems run on ITIL for incidents, problems and changes.

Let me give you an example. Zolvit was a live legal platform with service levels, and it still needed regular improvements. PaySFT, on the other hand, needed very fast releases under heavy deadline pressure.

So what did I do? First, protected time. Zolvit ran on Kanban, with support time ring-fenced and about 10% kept for improvements, so support and change never fought each other. Second, changes sorted by risk. Standard changes were pre-approved, and big or risky ones were reviewed. Third, automatic checks on every change: build, test and security scan. And fourth, after any big incident, a no-blame review, and the fix went back into the pipeline.

And the result? Zolvit met its service levels every month while improvements kept shipping. And PaySFT still delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days.

So for me, it's Scrum for new builds, Kanban for support, DevOps for releases, and ITIL for live systems. And DORA metrics to show speed and stability side by side.

Likely follow-up: "When Kanban instead of Scrum?"

Kanban for steady, unpredictable work, like support. Scrum for planned building, with clear sprint goals.

q: How do you support Sales and Pre-Sales? How do you balance winning a deal with realistic promises?
a:
I help win work by bringing delivery reality into the deal. Honest estimates, assumptions in writing, and real case studies. And honestly, I'd rather lose a deal than win one we can't deliver at a profit.

Let me give you an example. Pre-sales is part of my current job. At NeuSix, my work starts at pitching and budgeting. At Brane, I proved a solution for WIN Semiconductors before they made a bigger commitment. And at DP World, our delivery itself created new business.

So what did I do? First, I estimate from real data, not hope, and I put the assumptions, dependencies and risks right into the proposal. Second, I prove it before we go big. For WIN Semiconductors, I scoped a proof of concept and showed a global client it would work. Third, I grow accounts through delivery. At DP World, I turned problems raised in steering into four use cases, each with an ROI workbook. And fourth, I own the handover from sales to delivery, so nothing we promised gets lost.

And the result? WIN Semiconductors saw it work before they committed. And DP World grew by four new use cases, which became a package we could sell to other logistics clients.

So for me, the best sales tool is a delivery team that keeps its promises.

Likely follow-up: "Sales already promised an unrealistic date?"

I don't complain, I give options. Here's what we can deliver by that date, here's what the full scope needs, and here's the risk of each. Then Sales, the client and I agree it in writing.

q: How would you build a team to shape and deliver a new opportunity?
a:
Two stages, two teams. A small, senior team to shape and win the deal. Then a delivery team built around the agreed scope. And I keep one or two of the same people in both, so nothing gets lost in between.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we shaped four new computer vision use cases, and then, of course, we had to deliver them. So the proposal had to be believable, and the team had to be real.

So what did I do? First, I kept the shaping team small and senior. Me, a couple of architects who understood warehouse operations, and the people building the ROI models. Second, I built the delivery team around the scope: computer vision, data, cloud and application skills, a lead for each stream, and one plan. No dependence on any one hero. And third, continuity. One or two people who shaped the deal stayed on in delivery, so the thinking behind the solution didn't get lost.

And the result? Four use cases, each with an ROI workbook, a proposal worth X, and the first use case approved.

So for me, it's small and senior to win it, and well organised to deliver it. And I plan the onshore, offshore and seniority mix from day one, so the deal is profitable, not just winnable.

Likely follow-up: "How do you mix offshore and onshore?"

Client-facing roles sit near the client, most building and testing happens offshore, and there's a written handover every day between time zones.

q: A customer who has run a business for 15 years asks you to build an application. What would you do?
a:
I wouldn't start with the app. Somebody who's run a business for 15 years already has ways of working, data and habits that work. So my first job is to find the business problem the app has to solve, and protect what already works.

Let me tell you how I'd approach it. A 15-year business owner doesn't really want an app. They want their business to run better. Less manual work, fewer mistakes, more sales.

So what would I do? First, understand the business. I'd sit with the owner and with the people who'll use the app every day, and ask, what would make this useful to you on Monday morning? Second, agree one goal we can measure, like cut order processing time by X%. Third, a short paid discovery. Two to four weeks, and they get a clear scope, a clickable prototype, an estimate and the risks. And fourth, deliver in phases. A first version that fixes the biggest pain, live with real users in weeks. And with 15 years of data, I'd plan the data move carefully and run old and new side by side until people trust it.

And honestly, people matter as much as software. Long-serving staff have their own way of doing things. So I'd involve them early, train them, and pick a champion inside the business. That's how it worked with WIN Semiconductors, and at DP World, where talking to the real users turned the program around.

So for me, I measure success by their business numbers, not by how many features we ship.

Likely follow-up: "What if they already know exactly what they want?"

I still spend a short time checking it. Usually most of their list is right. And the part that isn't is exactly where the real value, or the real risk, sits.

q: Walk me through how you respond to an RFP.
a:
I treat an RFP like a delivery plan written early. We win by showing the client we understand their business problem better than anyone else, with a solution, a price and a team we can actually deliver.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my work starts at pitching and budgeting, so I'm in the proposal from the first conversation. Nobody hands me a deal after it's signed.

So what do I do? First, decide whether to bid at all. Does it fit us, can we win, can we deliver, and what's the commercial risk? A fast no is better than a slow loss. Second, read between the lines. I list what they asked for, then ask questions to find the business result behind it. That's usually where we stand out. Third, shape the solution with a small senior team: an architect, a subject expert and me, with Sales owning the relationship. Fourth, estimate from real data and write every assumption down. And finally, delivery, finance and legal review it before it goes out.

And the result? At DP World, we turned the client's operational problems into four computer vision use cases, each with an ROI workbook. So the proposal was about business value, not about technology.

So for me, the best proposal reads like the first chapter of a successful project.

Likely follow-up: "What's your win rate?"

It's around X%. But honestly, I look at win rate together with the margin of the deals we win. Winning work that loses money isn't success.

q: How do you estimate effort and cost for a proposal?
a:
I estimate from facts, not hope. I break the work down, check it against real past projects, show the uncertainty honestly, and write every assumption into the proposal.

Let me give you an example. When PaySFT lost half its team, the client needed to make a decision fast. I could give them a costed ₹32 lakh option to deliver everything within days. And I could only do that because our estimates came from real data.

So how do I do it? First, break it down. Big features become small tasks, and the people who'll build them estimate them, not only Sales. Second, check against the past. I know what 125 APIs and two mobile apps really took on PaySFT, and that's a better guide than any formula. Third, use ranges: best case, likely case and worst case, especially for AI, where data quality is the big unknown. Fourth, add the hidden work: testing, environments, security, knowledge transfer and support after go-live. That's what usually gets missed. And finally, write the assumptions down, so a change becomes a change request, not our loss.

And the result? Clients get a number they can trust, and we don't lose our margin halfway through.

So for me, an estimate is only as good as its assumptions. So I make them visible.

Likely follow-up: "Sales wants you to cut your estimate to win the deal?"

I show what would have to change to hit that price: less scope, phases, or different assumptions. I don't just cut the number and hope.

q: How do you choose the right commercial model: fixed price, time and materials, or outcome-based?
a:
I match the commercial model to how clear the scope is. Clear and stable scope can be fixed price. Unclear scope should be time and materials, or done in phases. And outcome-based only works when the result can be measured, and we can actually influence it.

Let me give you an example. At WIN Semiconductors, the scope had a real technical unknown. So instead of a big fixed price based on guesses, we started with a proof of concept, and showed it would work before the bigger commitment.

So how do I choose? Fixed price, when requirements are clear. We carry the risk, so the price must include it, with strict change control. Time and materials, for discovery, changing products, or AI work where nobody knows the answer yet. Phased, which is often the best for a new client: a fixed-price discovery first, then the build once the scope is clear. Outcome-based, linked to a business result like money saved, but only with an agreed starting point. And for live platforms like Zolvit, a managed service, linked to service levels.

And the result? The client takes less risk up front, and we don't sign up for a fixed price on guesses.

So for me, the wrong commercial model can turn a good project into a loss. So I choose it as carefully as the design.

Likely follow-up: "The client insists on fixed price for an uncertain AI project?"

I suggest a short fixed-price discovery to take out the biggest unknowns first. Then we fix the price for the build. That protects both sides.

q: When would you propose a proof of concept, and how do you make sure it converts into a real project?
a:
I only suggest a proof of concept when there's a real unknown, technical or business. And before we start, I agree two things in writing: what success looks like, and what happens next if it works. That's how it turns into a real project, and not free work.

Let me give you an example. At Brane, I scoped a proof of concept for WIN Semiconductors. They're a global client, and they needed to see it work on their own reality before committing more money.

So what do I do? First, I aim it at the biggest risk. The proof of concept answers one question, like can the model reach the accuracy we need on your data? Not a mini version of everything. Second, I fix the time and the team: a set number of weeks, a set number of people. Third, I agree success in writing, like accuracy above X% on their real data, signed off by their technical lead. And fourth, I agree the next step before we start: the next phase, the budget, and who decides.

And the result? At WIN Semiconductors, we proved it would work, and the client had the confidence to go further.

So for me, a proof of concept without agreed success and a next step is just free consulting. So I try to make it paid. Even a small fee means the client is committed.

Likely follow-up: "The client wants the POC for free?"

If the account really matters, I can put in some of our own effort. But I still insist on the success measures and the agreed next step. That's what protects both of us.

q: How do you differentiate your proposal against competitors?
a:
Competitors can usually match the technology, and often the price. What they can't match is a team that clearly understands the client's business, has done it before, and shows exactly how it'll manage the risk.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, every use case we proposed had an ROI workbook in the client's own numbers. So while others talk about technology, we were talking about money saved.

So what do I do? First, I open with their business problem and their numbers, not our services. Second, I show proof, not claims. Real results, like 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days on PaySFT. Third, I show how we'll reduce the risk: how we'll run the program, how we'll get the data ready, and how we'll decide on go-live. Senior leaders buy confidence. Fourth, I bring the delivery team to the pitch, so the client meets the people who'll actually do the work. And finally, I demo something real. On Philips, leaders saw a working digital twin, not slides, and that built trust really fast.

And the result? We compete on value and confidence, not on the lowest price.

So for me, clients don't buy the best solution. They buy the team they trust to deliver it.

Likely follow-up: "What if a competitor is much cheaper?"

I show the total cost, including risk, rework and delays, and I offer a phased option so they commit less money up front. I won't win by cutting quality to drop the price.

q: How do you manage delivery risk in the contract?
a:
A bad deal costs more than a lost one. So once we decide to bid, I make sure the contract matches the real delivery risk. We should never sign up for something we can't deliver at a profit.

Let me give you an example. On PaySFT, when we lost half the team, having a costed decision ready protected both our margin and the client's trust. The lesson I took into pre-sales is simple. Agree up front how changes like that will be handled, before anyone needs it.

So what do I do? First, I write the assumptions into the contract: the scope, what the client provides and by when, how work gets accepted, and what's out of scope. Second, change control. A clear process for changes and how we price them. Third, acceptance rules you can measure, so done is never a matter of opinion. On a takeover like Zolvit, I'd even write the handover checks into the contract. And fourth, liability and penalties, reviewed with legal, so we only take penalties on things we actually control.

And the result? When something changes mid-project, it's a conversation about the contract, not an argument about blame.

So for me, the cheapest time to fix a delivery risk is before the contract is signed.

q: How do you manage the handover from sales to delivery?
a:
Nothing we promise in the sale should get lost in delivery. So the delivery lead is in the deal before signing, and the handover is a formal step, not just an email.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, one or two of the people who shaped the four use cases stayed on to deliver them. So the thinking behind the solution, and the promises we made, didn't get lost.

So what do I do? First, delivery is part of the deal team. The delivery lead joins before the proposal goes in, so we only promise what we can deliver. Second, a proper handover pack: the signed scope, the assumptions, anything promised in meetings, the key client people and what they care about, and the known risks.
