q: Walk me through the cost of one Vigilant lead. How would you calculate it?
a:
Cost per lead is the sum of every model call and tool call for one lead. For each model call, it's input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price. On Vigilant, I tracked this from day one, because the client's pricing depended on it.

Let me walk you through it with illustrative numbers, not our real ones. Say research makes six calls of about 3,000 input and 500 output tokens, and drafting is one call of 2,000 in and 400 out. That's about 20,000 input and 3,400 output tokens per lead, plus web search and data provider calls. [Give your real cost per lead.]

So what did I do? First, I asked the team to build this cost model before launch, so we could price the service and not guess. Second, the model showed the research step's input was the biggest cost, so I prioritised the fixes: read fewer pages, extract facts first, use a cheaper model for extraction, and cache repeated prompt parts. Third, I put cost per lead into the commercial agreement and our weekly report, so the client and our finance team saw the same number.

And the result? The price covered the running cost, with no margin surprises.

So for me, if you can't write the cost formula for an AI feature, you can't price it or control it.

Likely follow-up: "How does cost change at 10 times the volume?"

It goes up roughly ten times, unless we use batch pricing, caching or volume discounts. That's why I model it before scaling, not after.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: Users say the AI is slow. How do you break down and reduce latency?
a:
I break it into parts, because slow could mean many things. Time to first token, which is how long before the user sees anything. Generation speed, in tokens per second. Retrieval time. Tool call time. And network and queueing.

Then I look at the p95, not the average. The average can look fine while one in twenty users waits far too long.

Then the fixes depend on where the time goes. If it's time to first token, a long prompt is often the reason, so shorter prompts and prompt caching help, and streaming the answer makes the wait feel much shorter. If it's generation, a shorter answer or a faster, smaller model. If it's retrieval or re-ranking, tune the index or re-rank fewer candidates. And for agents, the big one is usually sequential tool calls, so we run independent calls in parallel, and cut steps that don't add value.

[Give a real example, for example: on Vigilant, running searches in parallel cut the time per lead from X to Y seconds.]

So for me, measure each part, fix the biggest one, and stream so the user sees progress.

Likely follow-up: "What's a good latency target?"

It depends on the use. For a chat answer, users expect to see text within a second or two. For a background agent like lead research, a minute can be fine, as long as it doesn't block anyone.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: What is prompt caching, and what's the risk with caching answers?
a:
Prompt caching is when the model provider stores the processed version of the start of your prompt. If the next request starts with exactly the same text, like the same long system instructions or the same document, it reuses that work. You pay much less for those cached tokens, and the response starts faster. The trick is to put the stable parts first, and the changing parts, like the user's question, at the end.

Answer caching is different. You store the final answer and return it when the same question comes again. That's very cheap and fast for repeated questions. A semantic cache goes further and returns a stored answer when a new question is similar in meaning.

The risks are real, though. One, stale answers: if the source documents change, the cached answer is now wrong. So caches need expiry and must be cleared when content changes. Two, wrong matches: with semantic caching, two questions can look similar but need different answers, especially in legal work, where one word changes everything. Three, privacy: you must never return an answer built from one user's private data to another user.

So on something like Zolvit, I'd use prompt caching freely, and answer caching only for general questions, with strict rules. [Confirm what you used.]

So for me, cache the work, be very careful caching the answers.

Likely follow-up: "How would you set the similarity threshold for a semantic cache?"

Test it on pairs of questions that should and shouldn't match, and set it high. A cache miss costs a few cents. A wrong answer costs trust.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: On Philips, what exactly was the model predicting, and which algorithm did you use? Why that one?
a:
On Philips, the model predicted the probability that a key component of the X-ray machine would fail within the next X days, from sensor readings, logs and error codes. [Confirm the exact target.] The business goal was simple: warn early enough to plan a service visit before a hospital lost a machine.

The team used [name the algorithm, for example gradient boosted trees like XGBoost]. And I was part of that decision, because it wasn't only technical.

So what did I do? First, I set the criteria with the data scientists: it had to work with the limited number of real failures we had, and the service engineers had to understand why it raised an alert. Gradient boosted trees fit both, while deep learning needed far more failure data and was harder to explain. Second, I agreed a rule: start with the simpler, explainable model, and only fund a more complex one if it clearly beat it on the same test. Third, I made sure Philips' engineers saw which readings drove each prediction, which built trust in the model.

And the result? Philips passed all three stages against the agreed accuracy targets.

So for me, start with the simplest model that can win, and make complexity earn its budget.

Likely follow-up: "What were your most important features?"

[Give the real ones.] Typically things like temperature trends, how often specific error codes appeared in the last days, and usage counts since the last service.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: Failures are rare. How did you deal with class imbalance in training and evaluation?
a:
On Philips, failures were rare. If only 1% of cases are failures, a model that always says no failure is 99% accurate and completely useless. So the first decision I made with the team was that accuracy would never be our success measure.

Let me give you the context. Leadership naturally asks, how accurate is it? If we'd answered 99%, we'd have set the wrong expectation.

So what did I do? First, I agreed with the data scientists and the client to use precision, recall and the precision-recall curve as the success measures, and I explained them to leadership in plain words: how many failures we catch, and how many alerts are false. Second, I let the team choose the technical fixes, like class weights or careful resampling on training data only, and asked them to show me the effect on the test set [say what was used]. Third, I made sure the alert threshold was set with the service team, not left at a default.

And the result? [Give your precision and recall.] Expectations matched reality, and Philips passed all three stages.

So for me, with rare events, the most important decision is the metric, and that's a delivery decision, not just a data science one.

Likely follow-up: "Why not just use SMOTE?"

With time series, synthetic points can create patterns that never happen in real machines, and can leak information across time. Class weights and threshold tuning were safer.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: How did you make sure the Philips model wasn't cheating? How did you split the data?
a:
On Philips, I treated data leakage as a delivery risk, because it's the most common reason a model looks brilliant in testing and fails in the field.

Let me give you the context. Readings from the same X-ray machine look very alike, and time-series data makes it easy for a model to see the future by accident. If that happened, we'd report results to Philips leadership that the field would never match.

So what did I do? First, I made the data split a documented, reviewed decision: train on an earlier period and test on a later one, and test on machines the model had never seen. Second, I asked the team for a feature check: every feature had to be something we'd really know at prediction time. Third, before any results went to leadership, I insisted on a shadow-mode field trial: live predictions, recorded but not acted on, then compared with what actually failed.

And the result? [Give the shadow-mode results.] The numbers we showed leadership held up in the field.

So for me, if a model's results look too good, I ask about leakage before I put them on a slide.

Likely follow-up: "What's a sign of leakage?"

Test scores far higher than you'd expect, or one feature that's suspiciously powerful. When we see that, we check exactly when that feature becomes known.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: What were the precision and recall, and how did you choose the alert threshold with the service team?
a:
[Give the real numbers, for example: precision of X% and recall of Y% at our chosen threshold, with an average of Z days of warning.] But the more important story is how we chose that threshold, because I treated it as a business decision.

Let me give you the context. Lower the alert threshold and you catch more failures, but you send engineers on more false alarms. The data scientists could show the trade-off, but they couldn't decide it for Philips.

So what did I do? First, I brought the Philips service team and our data scientists together and put a cost on each mistake: a missed failure meant a machine down in a hospital and an emergency visit; a false alarm meant a wasted engineer visit. Second, we checked capacity: how many alerts the team could really act on each week. Third, we chose the threshold with the lowest total cost within that capacity, added a confidence level to each alert so the biggest risks went first, and wrote the threshold into the success criteria.

And the result? The service team trusted the alerts, because they had helped set the rules.

So for me, the people who act on the alerts should help set the threshold, and my job is to get them in the room.

Likely follow-up: "Did you use one threshold for all machines?"

[Confirm.] Often you start with one, then adjust for machines in critical hospitals, where a missed failure costs more.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: How do you monitor drift, for both the Philips model and an LLM app like Zolvit?
a:
For a classic model like Philips, there are two kinds of drift. Data drift, where the inputs change, for example new software on the machines changes how a sensor reports. And concept drift, where the link between inputs and failures changes, for example a new part design fails differently.

For data drift, we compare the live distribution of each important feature with the training data. Common measures are the population stability index, PSI, or a statistical test like Kolmogorov-Smirnov. If a feature moves past an agreed limit, we get an alert. For concept drift, you need the outcomes, so we tracked the real precision and recall as failures came in, month by month. Retraining was triggered by drift alerts or a drop in performance, not just by a calendar. [Confirm what was monitored.]

For an LLM app like Zolvit, drift looks different. User questions shift to new topics, the legal content changes, and the model provider may update the model. So we pin the model version, track the mix of question topics, watch retrieval scores and user feedback over time, and re-run the test set on a schedule and on every change.

So for me, a model starts getting older the day it goes live. Monitoring tells you when it needs attention.

Likely follow-up: "Would you retrain automatically?"

Automatic retraining, yes, but automatic deployment, no. The new model has to pass the same tests, and someone approves it before it replaces the old one.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: For the DP World damage detection model, how do you measure a computer vision model, and how do you run it on edge devices?
a:
For object detection, the engineers measure IoU, how well the predicted box overlaps the real one, and mAP, the average precision across damage types. That's the technical score. But at DP World, I insisted on a second, business score.

Let me give you the context. Damaged goods were being found too late, and that problem kept coming up in our steering meetings. The operations team didn't care about mAP. They cared about how many damaged items we caught and how many false alerts they had to check per shift.

So what did I do? First, I agreed two sets of success measures upfront: mAP for the engineers, and catches and false alerts per shift for operations. Second, because the model had to run near the cameras, I planned edge optimisation as its own step, like quantisation and an optimised runtime, with an accuracy re-check afterwards [name the hardware and tools, or say this was the proposed design]. Third, I took the results to the operations team through live demos, not slides.

And the result? [Give the target or real numbers.] And damage detection became one of the four computer vision use cases at DP World.

So for me, a vision model has to win with the engineers and with the people on the warehouse floor.

Likely follow-up: "How would you get enough examples of rare damage types?"

Collect hard cases from production, augment the images we have, and use active learning, where the model flags uncertain images for people to label first.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: Pressure test: I give you a RAG system that's right only 60% of the time. What do you check first?
a:
First, I'd stop everyone from guessing. A RAG system at 60% isn't one problem, it's three or four, and my job is making the team find out which ones before anyone changes anything. That's how we managed quality on Zolvit after we took it over.

So what would I do? First, I'd ask the team to take the failed answers and sort each into a bucket: the right information wasn't found, it was found but the model misused it, or the documents simply don't cover the question. Second, I'd prioritise fixes by how many failures each bucket explains. If it's retrieval, which it usually is, the fixes are chunking, keyword search and re-ranking. If it's the answer step, it's the prompt, the context size or a stronger model, tested on the failed cases only. Third, if the documents don't cover it, that's not a technical fix. I'd bring in the content owners, and make the system say I don't know meanwhile.

And then I'd agree a target with the business based on risk, and report progress against the test set every week. On Zolvit, our legal test set made this possible, because every fix was measured. [Give a real example of a fix and its effect.]

So for me, you fix RAG in order of impact, with data, and you keep the business informed every step.

Likely follow-up: "What target would you aim for?"

It depends on the risk. For a legal or medical assistant, very high on the questions it answers, and it should refuse when unsure. I'd agree the target with the business against the test set.

topic: AI Skills Interview: Deep Technical Probes (New)
q: Last one: the Philips model works well in testing, but the service engineers ignore the alerts. What do you do?
a:
That's not a model problem. It's a trust and workflow problem, and it's very common. A model nobody acts on has zero value.

First, I'd find out why, by talking to the engineers. Usually it's one of three things. They don't understand why the alert fired. They've had false alarms before and stopped believing it. Or the alert doesn't fit their workflow, it's in a separate dashboard nobody opens.

Then the fixes. Explain each alert: show the main signals behind it, for example using SHAP values, which show how much each feature pushed the prediction up or down, translated into plain words, like temperature has been rising for five days. Raise the threshold if false alarms are the issue, so fewer, better alerts rebuild trust. Put the alerts into the tools they already use, like their service ticket system. And close the loop: engineers mark each alert as useful or not, and that feedback improves the model.

That's why on Philips, approval from the service engineers was one of our formal success measures, not an afterthought. [Give a real example of feedback you acted on.]

So for me, AI success is measured by what people do with the output, not by the model's score.

Likely follow-up: "How would you measure trust?"

The share of alerts the engineers acted on, how quickly they acted, and the useful or not useful feedback on each alert, tracked month by month.

q: How do you ensure that multiple projects are delivered on time and within budget while maintaining quality standards? (Similar to a follow-up in question 9)
a:
I run every project on the same system, so problems with time, money or quality show up while they're still small. And then I spend my own time where the risk is highest.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run five programs at the same time, each with a different client, technology and deadline.

So what do I do? First, every program gets the same rhythm: a daily stand-up, a weekly review of schedule, spend and bugs, and a monthly steering meeting. Second, one risk list across all programs, with a name and a date on every item. Third, quality is built in, with automated tests from the start, not checked at the end. And fourth, when a project starts to slip, I step in early, before the milestone.

And the result? When PaySFT lost half its team, we caught it in week one and still delivered 125 APIs and two apps in 45 days. And Zolvit's live service was never affected.

So for me, a good system shows you problems while they're still cheap to fix.

Likely follow-up: "What do you keep for yourself, and what do you delegate?"

I keep client relationships, big risks and decisions on money or scope. Everything else goes to the leads, with clear ownership and a weekly check-in.

q: How do you plan capacity across feature delivery, support and improvement work? (Similar to question 10)
a:
I split the team's time on purpose, and I protect it. Because if improvement work has to fight support tickets every week, it simply never happens.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, our live legal platform, support tickets could easily have used up all of our time.

So what did I do? First, support and service levels always came first. Second, I split capacity clearly: support, change requests, urgent fixes, and about 10% kept only for improvements. Third, we picked improvements that reduce support work, like fixing the causes of repeat tickets. And fourth, we showed those improvements to the client every quarter.

And the result? The service stayed stable, we met service levels every month, and the client kept getting improvements, not just fixes.

So for me, improvement needs its own budget, even a small one, or the urgent work always wins.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client won't pay for improvement time?"

I show them what not improving already costs: the repeat tickets and the manual work. Usually the improvement pays for itself in a few months.

q: Delivery recovery: you take over a critical project that is already three months behind schedule. How would you recover delivery without compromising quality or team morale? (Similar to a follow-up in question 11)
a:
When a project is three months late, I don't push harder on a broken plan. I make the plan smaller and honest, I protect quality, and I look after the team.

Let me give you an example. On PaySFT, we lost about half the team, dates were slipping, and the client had escalated.

So what did I do? First, I took a short time to understand the real work left, and told the client honestly in week one. Second, I re-planned around the must-haves, for the team we actually had. Third, testing stayed in the plan, because testing is never the buffer. And fourth, I protected morale: a clear plan, blockers cleared every day, and no endless overtime as the plan.

And the result? 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days. The client trusted us again, and the team stayed.

So for me, a smaller, honest plan is what saves a late project.

Likely follow-up: "Would you add more people?"

Only as a last step. New people slow a team down for the first few weeks. So I cut scope and remove blockers first.

q: How do you manage a situation where a project is falling behind schedule and the client is expecting delivery as planned? (Similar to a follow-up in question 12)
a:
I tell the client early, with facts and options. Clients can accept a new plan. What they can't accept is a surprise on the delivery day.

Let me give you an example. On PaySFT, we lost half the team, but the client still expected the original plan.

So what did I do? First, I told them in writing in week one: what happened, why, and what we'd change. Second, I split the must-haves from the nice-to-haves, so the most important parts could still land on time. Third, I gave them a clear choice, including a costed ₹32 lakh option to deliver everything. So they decided with real facts.

And the result? We delivered in 45 days, the escalation closed, and the client trusted us again.

So for me, a missed date is a trust problem first, and a schedule problem second.

Likely follow-up: "What if the date really can't move?"

Then the scope moves. The must-haves go live on the date, and the rest follows in a planned second phase.

q: Multi-team dependency management: how would you manage delivery risks when multiple engineering teams, vendors and business units depend on one another, but none reports directly to you? (Similar to a follow-up in question 14)
a:
When the teams don't report to me, I lead with one shared goal and one plan everyone can see. Not with authority.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, four teams depended on each other, and some of them were outside our company, including Philips' own engineers.

So what did I do? First, I asked the sponsor to confirm the goal and my role, so everyone knew who was coordinating. Second, one shared goal, less machine downtime, and one plan for all four teams. Third, written agreements instead of orders, like our data agreement with Philips, with need-by dates and a 48-hour escalation rule. And for vendors, it was in the contract.

And the result? We passed all three stages on one plan.

So for me, when everyone sees the same plan every week, they hold themselves to it.

Likely follow-up: "What if a team still doesn't deliver?"

I go to that team's manager with the facts and the cost of the delay. If it still doesn't move, it goes to the sponsor, with options.

q: Executive stakeholder conflict: two senior stakeholders have conflicting priorities, and both consider their requirements business-critical. How would you align them and reach a decision? (Similar to a follow-up in question 15)
a:
When two senior leaders both say theirs is most important, I don't pick a winner. I put the facts side by side, and let the business decide.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, PaySFT urgently needed more people. But Zolvit, a live service, still needed its whole team.

So what did I do? First, I met each side separately, to understand the real business result behind the request. Often the conflict is in the solution, not the goal. Second, I put both options on one page: value, cost of delay, and risk. Third, my recommendation. Keep Zolvit's team, re-plan PaySFT, and give the PaySFT client a costed ₹32 lakh option.

And the result? PaySFT delivered in 45 days, and Zolvit was never affected.

So for me, priority comes from business value, not from rank.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still can't agree?"

I take both options to the leader they both report to, with my recommendation, and the decision is written down.

q: How do you manage resource allocation when multiple projects require the same critical team members? (Similar to a follow-up in question 15)
a:
I protect live services first, and for the rest I use a rule everyone agreed in advance. I never quietly move people from one project to rescue another.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my five programs share the same AI and cloud engineers. When PaySFT needed people, Zolvit still needed its support team.

So what did I do? First, I didn't touch Zolvit's team, because a live service comes before a new build. Second, I re-planned PaySFT for the team it actually had. Third, I gave the client a costed option instead of quietly borrowing people. And longer term, I train people across skills, so we never depend on one person.

And the result? Both projects came through fine.

So for me, priority comes from value, not noise.

Likely follow-up: "What if two leaders both say their project comes first?"

I show both options with the cost of delay, and take it to their common boss with my recommendation.

q: A product launch date is fixed but the scope is uncertain. How do you manage it? (Similar to question 16)
a:
If the date can't move, then the scope has to. So I make it very clear what must be live on the date, and what can follow.

Let me give you an example. At Jazeera Airport, the launch was tied to a leadership event, so the date was fixed. And two weeks before launch, live camera feeds for two of the six zones were blocked by approvals outside our control.

So what did I do? First, a clear 22-point go-live checklist, signed by each lead. Second, I suggested a phased launch: four zones live on the date, and recorded video for the other two. Third, the sponsor agreed it in writing, and we rehearsed twice with a backup.

And the result? We launched on the date with no issues, and all zones went live three weeks later.

So for me, don't fight the date. Change what goes live on it.

Likely follow-up: "How do you decide what the must-haves are?"

Together with the sponsor, based on the purpose of the launch. Whatever the launch event really needs is a must-have. Everything else goes to phase two.

q: What approach do you follow to manage client expectations and maintain long-term client relationships? (Similar to a follow-up in question 18)
a:
Three things: clear expectations at the start, no surprises along the way, and value beyond the contract.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, we worked with the operations team for a long time, and the relationship became very close.

So what did I do? First, we agreed up front what success looks like. Second, I always shared bad news early, with options. Third, I set up a weekly slot for small requests, so favours didn't turn into hidden work. And fourth, I listened for their next problems in every steering meeting.

And the result? The relationship grew into four new projects.

So for me, keep the goodwill, but keep the promises clear and visible.

Likely follow-up: "How do you handle an unhappy client?"

I listen, I own our part, and I agree a short recovery plan with dates. Trust comes back through results, not words.

q: How do you manage scope changes when a client requests additional features during an ongoing project? (Similar to a follow-up in question 20)
a:
I never just say no, and I never quietly do extra work for free. I give options, and I write the decision down.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, the client got used to sending quick requests on WhatsApp. One Thursday evening, they asked for a new dock layout and simulation by Monday.

So what did I do? First, I checked the impact on scope, time and the plan. Second, I gave them clear options: swap it for something of the same size, deliver a smaller version first, or add it as a paid change. Third, I set up a weekly slot for quick changes, with fixed capacity.

And the result? The client still got their changes, the hidden weekend work stopped, and the relationship got stronger.

So for me, changes are normal. It's unmanaged changes that break projects.

Likely follow-up: "What if the client says it was always in scope?"

We check the agreed scope together. If it's genuinely unclear, we agree a fair split and tighten the wording for next time.

q: Commercial accountability: a project is delivering successfully from a technical perspective, but its costs are exceeding the approved budget. How would you manage financial performance while protecting business outcomes? (Similar to a follow-up in question 22)
a:
If a project works well but costs too much, I find exactly where the money is going, and fix that first. Not the quality.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, we met every studio deadline. But costs were running 18% over plan.

So what did I do? First, I found that about 35% of our effort was going into rework. Second, we added our own review before anything went to the studio. Third, we automated the repeated steps. And fourth, we made sure every studio change was recorded and billed.

And the result? Productivity went up 20%, and costs came back to within 5% of plan. And the studios were happier.

So for me, cutting quality to save money is the most expensive mistake you can make.

Likely follow-up: "What if you still can't close the gap?"

I tell the sponsor early, with a forecast, and give a clear choice: more budget, less scope, or more time.

q: Predictability and risk forecasting: which delivery metrics would you use to predict future outcomes rather than simply report historical performance? How would you turn those insights into executive-level decisions? (Similar to a follow-up in question 23)
a:
I want numbers that warn me before things go wrong, not ones that tell me after. And every warning I show a leader comes with a decision I need from them.

Let me give you an example. At Discreet Arts, leaders heard about delays far too late, usually on delivery day.

So what did I do? First, I measured before I changed anything. Second, I watched the early signs: what we promised versus delivered, scope growing faster than work done, risks open too long, and bugs going up. Third, I gave leaders a range of likely dates from real data, with the decision I needed, like drop scope, add people, or move a date.

And the result? We saw delays two to three weeks earlier, and leadership meetings only dealt with real problems.

So for me, looking ahead gives you time to fix things.

Likely follow-up: "If you could track only one number?"

What we promised versus what we actually delivered.

q: How do you improve predictability without converting Agile teams into Waterfall teams? (Similar to a follow-up in question 23)
a:
Predictability comes from small pieces of work and real data, not from big plans. So you don't need Waterfall to be predictable.

Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, dates kept slipping, and people wanted more detailed plans.

So what did I do? First, I measured how long work really took. Second, we limited work in progress and made tasks smaller. Third, we tracked what we promised versus what we delivered, every sprint. And we used that data to forecast.

And the result? Delivery got about 30% faster, and dates became reliable.

So for me, measure the flow. Don't add paperwork.

Likely follow-up: "How do you give leadership a date without a Waterfall plan?"

I give a likely range from real delivery data, and update it every sprint. That's more honest than one fixed date.

q: How do you identify and manage delivery risks before they affect project outcomes? (Similar to a follow-up in question 24)
a:
I look for early warning signs, and every big risk has an owner and a trigger. A trigger tells you exactly when to act.

Let me give you an example. On Philips, early on, we built on guesses about the machine data, and it didn't match.

So what did I do? First, a signed data agreement became a day-one task on every program. Second, I watch for early signs, like dependencies with no date or risks that stay open too long. Third, clear escalation times: 48 hours, then five days, then steering.

And the result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier.

So for me, a risk list tells you what might happen. A trigger tells you when to move.

Likely follow-up: "Can you give an example of a trigger?"

If the vendor isn't in testing by the 15th, we switch to the backup and I call their account director.

q: Vendor performance crisis: a strategic vendor fails to meet critical milestones, putting a major product launch at risk. How would you manage contractual obligations, recovery planning and stakeholder communication? (Similar to a follow-up in question 25)
a:
When a vendor misses dates, I do three things together. I protect our contract position, I push hard for recovery, and I quietly prepare a backup.

Let me give you an example. At Deluxe, vendor delays put studio deadlines at risk, with several vendors on the same films.

So what did I do? First, I used the contract to settle arguments, not opinions. Second, one recovery plan across all vendors, with dates and daily tracking. Third, the studio always heard about risks from me first, with options.

And the result? We met every studio deadline.

So for me, it's facts and a backup plan, never surprises.

Likely follow-up: "What if the vendor still can't recover?"

Then I use the contract remedies and switch to the backup, like another vendor or doing it ourselves.

q: How do you measure AI in delivery? (Similar to question 28)
a:
I measure AI at four levels. Is it accurate? Is it used? What does it cost? And does it move a business number? Because if I only measure the model, I'm measuring a demo, not delivery.

Let me give you an example. I've delivered AI on Zolvit, Vigilant and the Philips digital twin, and this is the scorecard I use.

So what do I measure? First, quality. Before go-live, the AI is scored against an agreed test set. After go-live, real accuracy, and how often a person has to correct it. Second, use. How many people rely on it, and how often they accept what it gives. Third, cost. On Vigilant, we tracked the cost of every task from day one. And fourth, the business result, like hours saved or new leads, against a starting point.

And the result? On Vigilant, agents went live only after passing the agreed score, with accuracy above X%.

So for me, if you don't measure before, you can't prove anything after.

Likely follow-up: "Which of the four matters most to a CXO?"

The business result. But I report all four, because the other three explain why the result is moving or not.

q: What steps do you take to improve delivery efficiency and reduce operational costs without compromising quality? (Similar to a follow-up in question 60)
a:
I measure first, then I remove waste, and I check quality every time we get faster. Most cost hides in rework and waiting.

Let me give you two examples. At Hornbill, delivery was slow. At Deluxe, costs were 18% over plan.

So what did I do? First, at Hornbill, one priority list, one way in for requests, and limits on work in progress. Second, at Deluxe, less rework, with our own review before the studio. Third, automation of the repeated steps in both places.

And the result? Hornbill got about 30% faster. Deluxe came back within 5% of plan, with productivity up 20%.

So for me, efficiency comes from removing waste, not from squeezing people.

Likely follow-up: "Where do you look first?"

Rework and waiting time. That's where most of the money goes.

q: Can you take me through the technical architecture of one of your projects? (Similar to question 62)
a:
Let me use PaySFT, the real estate platform. We built 125 APIs and two mobile apps in 45 days. I'll take you from the phone to the database and back.

Here are the layers. One, the Broker and Buyer mobile apps and a web portal. Two, the entry point: a CDN and firewall, then an API gateway that checks logins and sends each request to the right service. Three, the 125 APIs, grouped into services by business area, like listings, leads, payments and notifications, running in containers. Four, data: a main database, a cache for speed, search for listings, and file storage for images. And five, a message queue for slow tasks, like notifications, so users don't wait. [Name the real tools you used.]

Across all layers, we had infrastructure as code, a pipeline with automatic tests and security scans, encryption, role-based access, and monitoring with alerts.

And my main focus as the delivery lead was the API contracts. We agreed them first, so the mobile and backend teams could build at the same time. That's a big reason we hit 45 days.

So for me, I don't write the code, but I understand the architecture well enough to see where the risk is.

Likely follow-up: "Why microservices and not a monolith?"

Separate services let small teams build and scale the busy parts on their own. For a small, simple app, I'd start with one well-organised application and split it later.

q: How do you report Agile delivery status to non-Agile executives? (Similar to question 71)
a:
Executives don't need to learn Agile. They need dates, money, risks and decisions, on one page.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, my CEO-level sponsors don't want to hear about story points or velocity.

So what do I do? First, I report milestones and business results, not sprints. Second, I give a range of likely dates from real data. Third, clear colour rules, and every red item comes with the decision I need. And the pack goes out two days before the meeting.

And the result? Steering meetings became short, useful, and focused on decisions.

So for me, speak the business language, and keep the Agile detail inside the team.

Likely follow-up: "What if an executive wants a fixed date for everything?"

A firm date for what's committed, and a range for the rest, updated every month.

q: Value versus velocity: your teams consistently meet sprint commitments, yet business stakeholders report that delivery isn't generating the expected value. How would you identify and address the underlying problem? (Similar to question 78)
a:
When velocity is green and value is red, the team is usually building the wrong things, very efficiently. So I stop measuring output, start measuring results, and reconnect the work to the business problem.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, on the warehouse digital twin, delivery was moving. But the business couldn't see the value. And when I dug in, I found why. Our sponsor was the innovation team, but the real users were warehouse operations, and we'd never properly involved them.

So what did I do? First, I went to the real users. I sat with the operations team and asked, what would make this useful to you on Monday morning? Second, every piece of work had to link to a business problem, with a measure the business agreed. If it didn't link to anything, it went down the list. Third, I changed what we reported. Velocity stayed as an internal planning tool, and steering focused on business results. And fourth, demos every two weeks with real users, on their own warehouse data.

And the result? Within two months, the operations head was coming to demos and asking for features. The program turned around, and it led to four new projects.

So for me, velocity tells you the team is busy. Only results tell you the business is better off.

Likely follow-up: "What if the product owner says the backlog is right?"

I bring the usage data and the result measure we agreed, and we look at it together with the sponsor. The data usually settles it.

q: Leadership under pressure: a high-performing delivery lead repeatedly misses commitments and blames external dependencies. How would you investigate the issue, establish accountability and improve performance? (Similar to question 79)
a:
I separate the facts from the story before I judge the person. Sometimes the dependencies really are the problem. Sometimes they're the excuse. Either way, managing them is the lead's job.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, I was brought in for six months because several programs were missing deadlines. The leads were capable people. But every slip seemed to have a reason outside their team.

So what did I do? First, the facts. I reviewed every program's plan, risks and delivery. And most slips came from risks that were known for weeks, but had no owner and no date. Second, private, direct conversations. I walked each lead through how one risk, left open for weeks, became the exact slip we were facing. Facts, not blame. And honestly, high performers respond well to that. Third, I made ownership clear. One risk list, a name and a date on every item, and one rule. A dependency outside your control is still your risk to manage, and raise early. And fourth, I fixed the real blockers at my level, like one staffing plan, so people stopped being moved between projects every day.

And the result? The leads started owning their risks. Leadership had one view they trusted by day 60, and weekly results by day 90.

So for me, you can't control every dependency. But you can always control how early you see it, and how fast you raise it.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still don't improve?"

After a fair, documented period of support, I move to a formal performance process with HR. Past performance earns patience, not an exemption.

q: Governance transformation: you join an organisation where delivery governance involves excessive reporting, frequent status meetings and slow decision-making. What changes would you introduce without losing executive visibility or control? (Similar to question 80)
a:
Governance should make decisions faster, not slower. So I keep the visibility, but I change where it comes from. Live data instead of manual reports. Exception reviews instead of status meetings. And clear decision rights.

Let me give you an example. At Discreet Arts, leaders only found out about problems on the delivery day, even with lots of meetings. And at NeuSix, status was being put together by hand across our teams and four vendors.

So what did I do? First, one source of truth. At NeuSix, Jira and Confluence became the one place for our teams and vendors, so nobody built status by hand. Second, early warning instead of reports. At Discreet Arts, I built a dashboard that turned amber when a team fell behind. Third, exception-only meetings. Steering only covered red and amber items and decisions, with the pack sent two days before. And fourth, clear decision rights: what the team decides, what I decide, and what goes to steering, with a 48-hour decide or escalate rule.

And the result? At Discreet Arts, we saw delays two to three weeks earlier. At NeuSix, we got one view of all programs, and reporting time dropped by about half.

So for me, executives don't want more reports. They want no surprises, and fast decisions.

Likely follow-up: "How do you make the change without leaders feeling they've lost control?"

I run the new view next to the old reports for a month. Once they trust it, we switch the old ones off.

q: Strategic leadership: your organisation must deliver a major transformation within six months, but resources are limited and priorities keep changing. How would you build a realistic delivery strategy, prioritise initiatives and ensure sustainable execution? (Similar to question 81)
a:
With six months and limited people, you can't do everything. So I anchor on a few big results, put my capacity where it matters most, and make every change in priority a clear decision, not a daily surprise.

Let me give you an example. At Cosmos-Maya, leadership gave me six months to stabilise several running programs. There was no budget for more people, people were moved between projects every day, and priorities kept changing.

So what did I do? First, I diagnosed before acting. I reviewed every program's goals, people, money and delivery, to find what was really causing the problems. Second, I focused the capacity we had. One staffing plan for all programs, so people stopped being moved around, and my strongest leads on the most important work. Third, I controlled change. One risk and decision list, with owners, so any new priority became a visible decision with a trade-off. And fourth, I delivered in steps: 30, 60 and 90 days, with a visible result at each step to keep everyone confident.

And the result? We had a health check by day 30, one trusted view by day 60, and weekly results against milestones by day 90. And predictability, quality and utilisation all improved within the six months.

So for me, in six months, the real strategy is deciding what not to do, and saying it early.

Likely follow-up: "What if leadership keeps adding priorities?"

I show the trade-off on one page: what the new item pushes out, and what it costs in time. The sponsor decides, and we write it down.

q: How do you deliver a roadmap when product priorities change every month? (Similar to question 81)
a:
When priorities change every month, I keep the goals steady, and handle the changes at one fixed time, through one door.

Let me give you an example. At Hornbill, requests came from everywhere, and the plan changed almost weekly.

So what did I do? First, one priority list, and one way in for every request. Second, goals set per quarter, with details only for the next few weeks. Third, changes reviewed once a month. And anything new pushes something else out, visibly.

And the result? Delivery got about 30% faster, and the roadmap became believable again.

So for me, change is fine. Unmanaged change is what kills a roadmap.

Likely follow-up: "What if a senior leader wants a change right now?"

I show what it pushes out. The sponsor decides, and we write it down.

q: How do you handle disagreements between technical teams and business stakeholders about delivery priorities? (Similar to question 82)
a:
I don't take sides. I turn the disagreement into a trade-off both sides can see, measured against the business result. And I set a rule, so the same argument doesn't come back every sprint.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, our live legal platform, the business wanted new features as fast as possible. The tech team wanted time to protect stability and fix the root causes of support issues. Honestly, both were right. And the argument came back at every planning session.

So what did I do? First, I made both cases concrete. The business showed the value and urgency of each feature. The tech team showed the risk to service levels if stability work was skipped. Second, we agreed a rule, not a one-time winner. Ring-fenced time for service work, about 10% for improvements, and the rest for features. Third, inside the feature time, the business owned the order, and the tech team flagged risks openly. And fourth, we reviewed the split together regularly, so either side could ask to change it with facts.

And the result? Zolvit stayed stable while improvements kept shipping. And planning stopped being a negotiation every time.

So for me, most priority fights end when both sides agree the rule before they argue the case.

Likely follow-up: "What if they still disagree on one item?"

I take both options, with the cost and the risk, to the sponsor with my recommendation. And we write the decision down.

q: How do you measure team performance and ensure accountability across different project teams? (Similar to question 83)
a:
I measure every team on the same small set of numbers, balancing speed, quality and commitments. And I make accountability visible with names and dates, not with pressure.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, I run five programs with different clients and technologies. And when I started, every lead reported progress differently. So it was hard to compare teams, or spot trouble early.

So what did I do? First, one scorecard for every team: what we promised versus what we delivered, how long work takes, bugs that reach the client, and risks past their date. Second, speed always paired with quality, like at Deluxe, where we tracked productivity and rework together, so nobody looked fast by shipping bugs. Third, visible ownership. One risk list across all programs, with a named owner and a date on every item. And fourth, the numbers are there to coach, not to punish. They start the conversation in the weekly review.

And the result? Today, I can see a team slipping in days, not at the milestone. At Hornbill, the same approach cut delivery time by about 30%. At Deluxe, productivity went up 20%.

So for me, accountability is easy when everyone sees the same facts, and the same rules apply to every team.

Likely follow-up: "How do you stop teams gaming the numbers?"

Every speed number is paired with a quality number. And we use the numbers to ask questions, never to punish.

q: Can you describe how you would handle a major production issue immediately after a project release while ensuring minimal business disruption? (Similar to question 84)
a:
First, get the service back. Then find the cause. Then make sure it can't happen again. And all the way through, the business hears from me early and often, with facts, not guesses.

Let me give you an example. On Zolvit, a live legal platform, an outage isn't just technical. It's a risk to the client's reputation. So we prepared for incidents before we ever needed to.

So what do I do? First, prepare before the release: a tested rollback plan, monitoring and alerts, runbooks, and the top incidents rehearsed. Second, restore first. One incident lead takes charge, we check the business impact, and we roll back or switch the feature off if that's the fastest way back. The root cause can wait. The business can't. Third, a fixed communication rhythm. The sponsor hears from me within the hour, then updates every 30 minutes, with impact, actions and the next update time. And fourth, a no-blame review within a few days, a proper fix, and the lesson fed back into our tests and release checklist.

And the result? Zolvit stayed stable, and every major issue made our pipeline better. And I always plan a support period after go-live, like at Jazeera Airport.

So for me, in an incident, fast recovery and clear communication matter far more than finding someone to blame.

Likely follow-up: "Would you roll back or fix forward?"

Roll back by default, if that's the fastest safe way to restore service. I only fix forward if the fix is small, tested and quicker than a rollback.

q: How do you prove the business value, or ROI, of an AI program to a CXO? (Similar to questions 28 and 55)
a:
I prove it in the client's own numbers, against a starting point we measured before the AI went in. Not with model accuracy, and not with how many people logged in.

Let me give you an example. At DP World, every computer vision use case had an ROI workbook in the client's numbers. And on Vigilant, we tracked the cost of every task from day one, so we always knew what the AI was costing.

So what do I do? First, measure the starting point: hours, errors, delays, and what they cost. Second, agree one business number the AI should move, and by how much. Third, show the full cost, including the running cost of the AI, not just the build. And fourth, report the result every month against the starting point, together with accuracy, usage and cost, so the CXO can see why it's moving.

And the result? The conversation is about payback, not technology.

So for me, if you don't measure before, you can't prove anything after.

Likely follow-up: "What if the ROI isn't there after three months?"

We look at which of the four levels is failing, accuracy, usage, cost or the business process, and fix that. If it still doesn't pay back, we stop or narrow it. Stopping early is a good result too.

q: How do you keep client data safe when your team uses AI tools like Copilot? (Similar to question 27)
a:
I set the rules before anyone starts, not after something goes wrong. Approved tools only, no confidential data in public tools, and a person reviews everything the AI produces.

Let me give you an example. At NeuSix, our teams wanted AI coding assistants on client work, and we were handling client code and data.

So what did I do? First, only business licences, where the provider doesn't train on our data, and the client's okay where needed. Second, no confidential data in free or public tools. Third, every AI-written change goes through the same code review, tests and security scans. And fourth, we wrote these rules down and agreed them with the client.

And the result? The client was comfortable with us using AI, and we had zero data incidents.

So for me, AI speed only counts if the client can trust it.

Likely follow-up: "What if a developer breaks the rules?"

We treat it like any security incident: contain it, tell the client if their data was involved, and fix the gap. Then we retrain the team.

q: What is RAG, in one minute? (Similar to question 103)
a:
RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, means that before the model answers, we search the company's own documents for the relevant parts and give them to the model with the question. Then it answers from those sources, with citations. It's an open-book exam instead of a memory test.

On Zolvit, that's exactly how the legal platform worked. And as a delivery manager, I liked RAG because it's governable: the content can be updated without retraining, every answer can be checked against its source, and access rules can be respected.

So for me, RAG is the default way to make an LLM useful and trustworthy on a company's own data. And on Zolvit, good retrieval mattered more than the choice of model.

Likely follow-up: "What's the most common reason RAG fails?"

Retrieval. If the right document isn't found, the model can't give the right answer.

q: What is an AI agent? (Similar to question 26)
a:
An AI agent is an LLM that doesn't just answer. It takes actions to complete a task: it picks a step, uses a tool like a search or a database, looks at the result, and decides the next step.

On Vigilant, our agents researched sales leads and drafted outreach. As the delivery lead, I set the guardrails: read-only tools for research, limits on steps, time and cost, and a person approving every email before it went out.

So for me, an agent is like a new team member: useful, but it needs clear limits, supervision and a budget.

Likely follow-up: "What's the difference between an agent and a chatbot?"

A chatbot talks. An agent acts. That's why agents need permissions, limits and human approval.

q: Explain a scenario where your team was going through technical challenges, and how you solved the problem. (Similar to questions 33 and 77)
a:
Let me take one from the Philips X-ray digital twin, because it was a real technical problem, not just a schedule one. The AI model and the machine data didn't fit together, and integration kept failing.

Here's what happened. To keep moving while the real machine data wasn't ready, the team built the data pipeline and the first model features on assumed data formats. When real data started arriving from the machines, the field names, units and timestamps were different, some sensors reported at different rates, and there were gaps. So the pipeline broke, the features were wrong, and the model's early results couldn't be trusted.

So what did we do? First, we stopped guessing. We sat with the Philips engineers and signed a data agreement on fields, formats, units and timing. Second, we built validation into the pipeline: every batch was checked against that agreement, and bad data went to quarantine instead of into the model. Third, we lined up the sensors on a common time scale, handled short gaps, and flagged long ones. Fourth, we re-ran feature engineering and retrained on the clean data, and the data and AI teams tested integration together every week instead of at the end.

And the result? Integration problems showed up in weekly reviews, not at the end, we won back most of the lost time, and the program passed all three stages. [Add the real numbers, for example X weeks lost and Y recovered.]

So for me, most AI problems are data problems. Now every program I run starts with a data agreement and automated data checks on day one.

Likely follow-up: "What would you do differently?"

Sign the data agreement and get real sample data before building anything, and let the team build against that agreed format instead of guesses.
